## The statement

Wigner's 1939 theorem [@wigner1939] can be compressed to one sentence:

> An elementary particle *is* a unitary irreducible representation of the
> Poincaré group.

Unpacking it is most of a first course in QFT. The space of states of a
relativistic quantum system is a Hilbert space $\hilb$. Special relativity says
the Poincaré group $\mathrm{ISO}^+(1,3)$ — Lorentz transformations together with
spacetime translations — acts on physical states. Quantum mechanics says that
action must preserve transition probabilities $\abs{\braket{\phi}{\psi}}^2$,
and Wigner's earlier theorem says any such symmetry is implemented by a unitary
(or antiunitary) operator, unique up to phase. So $\hilb$ carries a projective
unitary representation of Poincaré. "Elementary" means the representation cannot
be broken into smaller invariant pieces: it is **irreducible**.

## What the classification says

Irreducible unitary representations are labelled by the eigenvalues of the
Casimir operators — the elements of the universal enveloping algebra that
commute with everything. For Poincaré there are two:

$$
P^2 = P_\mu P^\mu = m^2, \qquad
W^2 = W_\mu W^\mu = -m^2\, s(s+1),
$$ {#eq-casimirs}

where $P_\mu$ generates translations and $W_\mu = \half \eps_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}
J^{\nu\rho} P^\sigma$ is the Pauli–Lubanski vector. The first label in
@eq-casimirs is the **mass**, the second is the **spin**. For $m > 0$ the
little group fixing a rest-frame momentum is $\SO(3)$ — really its cover
$\SU(2)$ — and $s \in \set{0, \half, 1, \tfrac32, \dots}$. For $m = 0$ the
little group is the Euclidean group of the plane and the physical
representations are labelled by **helicity** instead. The appearance of
$\SU(2)$ rather than $\SO(3)$ is exactly the
[double cover](../lie-theory/su2-covers-so3.qmd) at work.

## What has to be understood first

Reading the statement with full understanding requires, in roughly this order:

1. **Lie groups and Lie algebras**, so that "Poincaré group" and "generators"
   are precise objects and $\comm{J_{\mu\nu}}{P_\rho}$ is a computation rather
   than a postulate.
2. **Unitary representations and irreducibility**, including Schur's lemma,
   which is why Casimirs act as scalars on irreducibles.
3. **Covering groups and projective representations**, to see why
   $\SL(2,\C)$ replaces $\SO^+(1,3)$ and where half-integer spin enters.
4. **Induced representations** (Mackey's method of the little group), which is
   how the infinite-dimensional unitary representations of a non-compact group
   are actually constructed from finite-dimensional ones of a subgroup.

Items 1–3 are the subject of the Lie theory section. Item 4 is where the
mathematics gets properly new.

## References to come back to

Woit [@woit2017, ch. 42] gives the cleanest mathematical treatment at this
level. Weinberg's *Quantum Theory of Fields*, vol. I, ch. 2 is the standard
physics account.
